description: Stable 3-tier grammar taxonomy for classifying TOEFL ITP Structure (Part A) and Written Expression (Part B) items: primary_target (closed set, do not expand casually) -> subtype (free-form, specific construction) -> secondary_features (free-form tags for co-occurring but non-primary grammar phenomena). Also documents the shared tested_error_type / distractor error_type closed vocabulary used by both sections.

tiers.primary_target: Closed set of 10-15 stable syntactic categories (currently 15, at the practical ceiling). New categories should only be added if a phenomenon recurs across 3+ items across multiple Practice Tests, does not fit as a subtype of an existing category, and forcing it into an existing category would meaningfully distort that category's definition.
tiers.subtype: Free-form string describing the exact tested construction within a primary_target. May grow without limit.
tiers.secondary_features: Array of free-form short tags describing co-occurring grammar phenomena that are not the primary test point of the item.
tiers.tested_error_type: Closed set of 15 values shared by Structure's distractors.*.error_type and Written Expression's error_span.tested_error_type. Describes the structural mechanism of an error/distractor, orthogonal to primary_target (which describes the grammar topic being tested). See tested_error_types below.

primary_targets.description: Whether an independent clause (subject + finite verb) is correctly formed; distinguishing fragments/run-ons; basic subject-verb agreement.
that-clauses and embedded/indirect questions functioning as subject, object, or complement; typically tests word order (no inversion) inside the clause.
Restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses: relative pronoun choice/case, clause-internal parallelism, correct verb after the relative pronoun.
example_subtypes: non-restrictive relative clause with parallel coordinate predicate
restrictive relative clause with correct relative pronoun

primary_targets.description: Internal structure of time/cause/concession/condition/purpose subordinate clauses (full clause vs. phrase vs. inverted form). Use CONNECTORS_CONJUNCTIONS when the focus is choosing among connector words instead.
Choosing the correct linking word/phrase among conjunction/preposition/adverb options expressing cause, contrast, comparison, etc. (e.g. due to / because / in spite of / regardless of).
example_subtypes: contrast connector selection (although vs. despite vs. however)

primary_targets.description: Tense, aspect, and active/passive voice selection for the finite main verb of a clause. Use NONFINITE_VERB_PHRASES for participle/infinitive/gerund form selection.
example_subtypes: past perfect vs. simple past selection
active vs. passive voice in main clause

primary_targets.description: What correctly follows a linking verb (predicate nominative/adjective) or a causative/perception verb (object complement).
example_subtypes: predicate nominative after linking verb (be + NP)
object complement after causative verb (make + O + Adj)

primary_targets.description: Form selection for participles (reduced relative clauses, result participles), infinitives (purpose, modifying ordinal/superlative nouns), and gerunds.
example_subtypes: reduced passive relative clause (past participle modifying noun)

primary_targets.description: Comparative/superlative structures and degree constructions (enough, so, too, as...as).
Syntactic parallelism among elements joined by coordinating or correlative conjunctions (and, or, both...and, not only...but also) or in a list.
example_subtypes: parallel verb forms in a list

primary_targets.description: Internal word order of noun-modifying elements: adjective phrases, appositives, participial modifiers, noun phrase structure itself.
example_subtypes: appositive noun phrase placement and internal word order
noun + postpositive adjective phrase word order
adjective order within a noun phrase

primary_targets.description: Subject-auxiliary inversion triggered by fronted negative adverbials, place adverbials, or elliptical conditionals.
example_subtypes: subject-auxiliary inversion after fronted negative adverbial ('Not until...')

primary_targets.description: Expletive 'there + be' and 'it + be' constructions and the errors that arise from substituting a referring pronoun or bare determiner.
Pronoun-antecedent reference/agreement, articles, quantifiers (much/many, few/little, every/each), and countable/uncountable noun choice.

Which derivational/part-of-speech form of a word (adjective/adverb/noun/verb) a given syntactic slot requires - whether the slot is a noun-phrase-internal modifier, the head noun of a phrase, a verb-modifying adverbial, or a clause subject - when the error is not about element ordering (WORD_ORDER_MODIFICATION), required verb complementation (VERB_COMPLEMENTATION), or clause well-formedness (CLAUSE_STRUCTURE) as such. Added 2026-08-23; see GRAMMAR_TAXONOMY_CHANGELOG.md.
example_subtypes: adjective required, adverb used to modify a following noun
adverb required, adjective/noun used to modify a verb
noun required, adjective used as clause subject
derivational noun-for-verb confusion as head of a prepositional-object phrase
ordinal number form required, cardinal used to modify a noun

tested_error_types.description: Incorrect tense/aspect/form (base/-ing/-ed etc.) of a verb.
A required element (subject, verb, connector, etc.) for the sentence/clause/phrase to be complete is missing.
An unnecessary or duplicated element is added.
All required elements are present but their order is wrong.
Wrong subordinating conjunction for the intended semantic/syntactic relation.
Wrong relative pronoun/marker choice or case (who/whom/which/that/whose).
Does not form a complete clause (missing finite verb or subject).
Subject is redundantly duplicated (e.g. relative pronoun plus a resumptive pronoun).
Subject-verb number agreement, or noun-quantifier agreement, error.
The complement structure (part of speech / phrase type) required by a linking or causative/perception verb is wrong. Does not cover fixed preposition collocations - see wrong_preposition_collocation.
The word's part of speech itself is wrong. Does not cover comparative/superlative confusion - see wrong_degree_form.
Pronoun has no clear or appropriate antecedent.

A fixed lexical preposition collocation governed by a verb/participle/adjective/noun is violated, or a standalone (non-governed) preposition/connector pairing is wrong (e.g. 'benefit from' vs 'benefit of', 'beside' vs 'between'). Not a part-of-speech error and not a clause-structural complementation mismatch - a lexical collocation slip. Added 2026-08-23; see GRAMMAR_TAXONOMY_CHANGELOG.md.

Comparative/superlative/positive degree confusion (e.g. superlative used where a comparative is required), or wrong degree/intensity marker for a construction that requires one (e.g. 'very' used where 'so' is required to license a following result clause). Added 2026-08-23; see GRAMMAR_TAXONOMY_CHANGELOG.md.
